source.title: The Weight Norm Sets the Grokking Timescale: A Causal Delay Law
source.authors: Xuan Khanh Truong; Viet Hoang Doan; Trung Duc Luu; D. Phan

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; PDF extraction causes some equation and layout artifacts, but the reported results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It tests delayed generalization on modular addition using the train/test-accuracy grokking measure, but its main intervention is a sustained weight-norm clamp rather than the original studies’ methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own grokking measurements and interventions. Results cited from other studies are not included as rows. It does not report whether time to grok grows as the training set shrinks; its training-fraction sweep reports critical norms, not grokking times. The Fourier-concentration result is temporal alignment, not a direct intervention on circuits.
record.test_reason: A sustained weight-norm clamp on modular addition, attention models and sparse parity tests whether the training regime (weight norm, weight decay, rescaling) sets the grokking delay (V3). Its Fourier-concentration trajectory bears weakly on V2. Grokking is taken as the setting: no row quantifies the train–test gap or how it depends on training-set size, so V1 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is largely correct. The authors conclude that the weight norm causally sets the grokking timescale. Networks grok at whatever norm they are held at, and the delay is exponential in the held relative norm, with a shared exponent across moduli. Apparent 'prevention' is the finite-budget tail of this law, and the norm dominates the learning rate (≈19× vs ≈2×). The effect recurs on an un-normalized attention model, is broken by LayerNorm, and is only partly reproduced on sparse parity. The link to Fourier circuits is temporal, not causal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses modular addition and train/test accuracy to measure grokking, but adds matched-counterfactual, sustained per-step norm clamps and studies the delay as a function of held norm.
record.method_sensitivity: Delay changes with held norm and learning rate; the norm-delay law saturates at high norm and has a low-norm floor for the smallest modulus. The effect is weak for one-shot rescaling, depends on whether LayerNorm decouples weight scale from function scale, and the exponent differs between the MLP and unnormalized attention model.

fits_no_version.finding: Under a sustained clamp the network groks at whatever norm it is held at. T_grok rises exponentially in the relative norm, with shared alpha≈7.5 across p (MLP) and ≈15 (attention), saturating beyond rho≈1.15–1.25.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking delay is an exponential function of the held weight norm relative to a critical norm.

fits_no_version.finding: Under free training, norm at grokking is concentrated (CV 1–2% across training fractions; <1% across 10× learning rate). It is set by weight decay and scales as p^0.38. On parity it recurs but drifts with data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking occurs at a concentrated, weight-decay-set critical weight norm.

record.problems: The exponential delay law is established over finite norm ranges and saturates at high norm. The smallest-modulus, low-norm condition does not grok within budget. The circuit account is supported only by temporal alignment, not direct intervention. The paper does not report the effect of training-set shrinkage on grokking time.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the further free-training observations of critical norm across training fractions, learning rates, and moduli because they do not report the claimed training-set-size dependence of grokking time. Also omitted LayerNorm norm-concentration and group-clamp findings because they concern norm observables and function-scale decoupling rather than the versions’ delayed-generalization outcomes.

untested.parts: Neither the size of the train–test gap (T_mem is never reported per condition) nor the growth of the delay as the training set shrinks is reported. Grokking is the assumed setting.
No circuit identification or intervention, no removal of memorizing components, no quantified lead of a progress measure before the jump.
Non-algorithmic data (images, text, molecules) and the lazy-to-rich transition.
All: no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
Efficient-circuit competition, critical dataset size, ungrokking.
All: optimizer and float artifacts are not examined.

missing.what: An Omnigrok-style low-norm initialization is washed out: the norm relaxes back and grokking occurs on the free timescale.
On the LayerNorm attention model, single-group clamps, including on the unembedding, shift grokking only weakly (up to ~2×). These were wrongly excluded in rows_left_out.
At lambda=3 the grokking time changes seven-fold across a 10× learning-rate range, while the norm at grokking is unchanged.
Free-training T_grok and T_mem across training fractions alpha 0.30–0.65 are not tabulated, only the norms. These would be needed for V1 set-size dependence.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked every clamp row to V1. These rows measure how an imposed norm changes T_grok, not the V1 effect, so V1 is moved to untested. The partial states on r13 and r15 reflected censoring, not effect size. The study's main bearing is on V3's 'set by weight norm/initialization' part: sustained norm control supports it, while one-shot and initialization rescaling challenge it. Weight decay and the norm clamp may count as one regime knob; the paper says the below-norm speed-up is indistinguishable from stronger regularization.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests delayed generalization on small algorithmic tasks, but does not report whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks.

It measures Fourier concentration over training and reports temporal alignment with grokking; it does not directly identify or manipulate circuits, show memorizing components being removed, or establish that a progress measure anticipates the test-accuracy jump.
It tests initialization rescaling and sustained norm clamps on algorithmic tasks, but not realistic non-algorithmic datasets such as images, text, or molecules, nor a lazy-to-rich transition.
No LLM pretraining or realistic-data fine-tuning is tested.
The paper does not test whether an efficient generalizing circuit displaces memorization, or the proposed critical-dataset-size and ungrokking predictions.
It does not compare the identifiable algorithms learned across runs.
It does not test adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point softmax limits as causes of grokking.
